claims.claim: Object-oriented programming is a paradigm that organizes a program around objects, which bundle related data (attributes/fields) together with the behavior (methods) that operates on that data.
A class is a blueprint or template that defines the attributes and methods shared by a kind of object; an object (instance) is a specific value created from that class, with its own state.

An attribute is a named value associated with an object (its data/state); a method is a function defined inside a class that, when called on an instance, receives that instance as its first argument (self in Python).
Encapsulation is bundling an object's data together with the methods that act on it and restricting direct outside access to that internal state (information hiding).
Inheritance lets a new (derived/child) class reuse and extend the attributes and methods of an existing (base/parent) class.
Polymorphism lets a single method name or interface work across different types, with each type supplying its own behavior.
As an OOP pillar, abstraction means exposing an object's essential features and behavior while hiding implementation detail; the broader idea of abstraction is developed in its own topic.

The 'four pillars' framing (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction) is a common teaching convention rather than a single, universally agreed definition of OOP; sources note there is no one accepted definition of the paradigm.
OOP contrasts with procedural programming, which organizes a program around procedures/functions that act on data kept separate from them rather than bundling data and behavior into objects.
OOP is supported by many languages and is not tied to one; terminology varies (Python 'attribute' vs C++ 'data member'; 'method' vs 'member function').
In Python, a class is instantiated with function-call notation (e.g., a = Account(100)); if the class defines __init__, instantiation automatically calls it to initialize the new instance's state.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether OOP has a fixed set of defining 'pillars.'
positions: Common teaching materials enumerate exactly four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
Reference sources note there is no single agreed-upon definition of OOP, and language features vary; some lists add 'information hiding' or 'dynamic dispatch' as separate items.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present the four pillars as a widely used teaching convention, define each correctly in one to two sentences, and state plainly that it is a convention, not a universal formal definition.

sourceRecords.title: The Python Tutorial — 9.2 Python Scopes and Namespaces
sourceRecords.notes: The Classes chapter (docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html). States 'Classes provide a means of bundling data and functionality together' and that creating a class creates a new type whose instances can be made; a method is 'a function that belongs to an object'; data attributes 'spring into existence when they are first assigned to'; class instantiation uses function notation and, when __init__ is defined, calls it automatically to initialize the new instance. Supports the bundling claim, class/instance distinction, attributes/methods, and the Python instantiation claim. Fetched and read directly.

sourceRecords.title: Python Documentation — Glossary (immutable, mutable, namespace, object)
sourceRecords.notes: Glossary entries used here: class = 'A template for creating user-defined objects'; object = 'Any data with state (attributes or value) and defined behavior (methods)'; method = 'A function which is defined inside a class body ... will get the instance object as its first argument (usually called self)'; attribute = 'A value associated with an object which is usually referenced by name using dotted expressions.' Supports the class/object/attribute/method definitions. Fetched and read directly.

sourceRecords.title: Object-oriented programming
sourceRecords.notes: Defines OOP as a paradigm based on objects that encapsulate data and functions; an object is an instance of a class; emphasizes encapsulation/information hiding, inheritance, dynamic dispatch, and polymorphism; notes there is no clear, agreed-upon definition of OOP and that features vary by language; mentions procedural programming as an alternative style. Supports the paradigm definition, class-vs-instance point, pillar definitions, the 'no single agreed definition' nuance, and the procedural contrast. Used REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.
